description: How heating changes state, internal energy and specific heat capacity.
content_html:
States of Matter and the Particle Model

All matter is made of tiny particles. The particle model helps explain how the same substance can exist as a solid, liquid or gas depending on how much energy its particles have.

In a solid, particles are held tightly in a regular lattice by strong forces of attraction. They vibrate but cannot move from place to place, which gives solids a fixed shape and volume. In a liquid, particles are still close together but the forces between them are weaker — they can slide past each other, so the liquid takes the shape of its container while keeping a definite volume. In a gas, particles are far apart and move rapidly in all directions, exerting pressure as they collide with the walls of their container.

Key Fact

Solid: particles vibrate in fixed positions — definite shape and volume. Liquid: particles slide past each other — definite volume, no fixed shape. Gas: particles move freely and rapidly — no fixed shape or volume, exerts pressure on its container.

Internal Energy

The internal energy of a substance is the sum of all the kinetic energy of its moving particles and all the potential energy stored in the forces between those particles. When you supply energy to a substance by heating it, the internal energy increases — the particles move faster or their arrangement changes, or both.

The temperature of a substance is a measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles. Raising the temperature means the particles are, on average, moving faster. However, during a change of state, temperature stays constant even though energy is still being supplied. This is because the energy goes into overcoming the forces between particles rather than speeding them up.

Specific Heat Capacity

Different materials need different amounts of energy to achieve the same temperature rise. Specific heat capacity (symbol \(c\)) is the quantity of energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. A high specific heat capacity means the substance stores a large amount of energy per kilogram for each degree of temperature rise.

The relationship between energy, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change is:

$$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta T$$

Where \(\Delta E\) is the change in internal energy in joules (J), \(m\) is the mass in kilograms (kg), \(c\) is the specific heat capacity in J/kg°C, and \(\Delta T\) is the temperature change in °C.

Worked example: An electric heater warms 2.0 kg of water from 20°C to 80°C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg°C. Calculate the energy transferred.

\(\Delta T = 80 - 20 = 60\)°C

\(\Delta E = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 60 = 504\,000\) J = 504 kJ

Always state the unit in your final answer. Check that all values are in SI units before substituting.

Key Fact

Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg°C — one of the highest of any common material. This means the sea absorbs large amounts of energy in summer and releases it slowly in winter, moderating coastal climates compared to inland areas.

Latent Heat

When a substance changes state, energy must be supplied (to melt or boil) or released (to freeze or condense) even though the temperature stays constant. This hidden energy is called latent heat. The word “latent” means hidden — the energy is used to break or form bonds between particles rather than raising the kinetic energy of particles.

There are two types: the specific latent heat of fusion (solid ↔ liquid) and the specific latent heat of vaporisation (liquid ↔ gas). The latent heat of vaporisation is always larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance, because changing from liquid to gas requires all the intermolecular forces to be overcome, not just weakened.

The energy for a change of state is calculated using:

$$E = m \times L$$

Where \(E\) is energy in joules, \(m\) is mass in kilograms, and \(L\) is the specific latent heat in J/kg.

Worked example: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 334 000 J/kg.

\(E = 0.5 \times 334\,000 = 167\,000\) J = 167 kJ

To measure specific heat capacity in school, a known mass of material is heated electrically. Record the current, voltage, time and temperature rise: \(\Delta E = V \times I \times t\), then \(c = \Delta E \div (m \times \Delta T)\). Insulate the sample to reduce heat losses to the surroundings.

Key Fact

Energy for a change of state: \(E = mL\). During a change of state temperature remains constant — all energy goes into breaking or forming bonds between particles, not into changing their kinetic energy. Latent heat of vaporisation is always greater than latent heat of fusion.

Density and Changes of State

Density is mass divided by volume: \(\rho = m / V\). When a substance changes state, the mass is conserved but the volume usually changes — so the density changes too. Gases have much lower density than liquids because the particles are far apart. An important exception is water: ice is less dense than liquid water because the particles in ice form a structure that takes up slightly more space than liquid water particles, which is why ice floats.
exam_tip_html: In questions about heating curves, make sure you can explain why temperature stays flat during a change of state — the common error is to say “the substance is not gaining energy.” It is gaining energy; that energy is being used to break bonds between particles (latent heat), not raise temperature. In calculation questions, check whether the question asks for specific heat capacity (use \(\Delta E = mc\Delta T\)) or latent heat (use \(E = mL\)) — mixing them is the most common multi-step error.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The particle model explains the three states of matter: solids have particles in fixed positions; liquids allow sliding motion; gases have freely moving particles that exert pressure on their container.
  • Specific heat capacity (\(c\)) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1°C; use \(\Delta E = mc\Delta T\). Water’s high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C) makes it effective for thermal storage.
  • Latent heat (\(E = mL\)) is the energy for a change of state at constant temperature; the latent heat of vaporisation is always greater than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance.

practice_questions.text: Define specific heat capacity and explain why water is used as a coolant in car engines despite its relatively high cost compared with other fluids.
practice_questions.marks: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (1). Water's high specific heat capacity means it absorbs a large amount of energy per kilogram before its temperature rises significantly, making it effective at removing heat from the engine (1).

practice_questions.text: A 0.80 kg block of aluminium is heated electrically. The heater supplies 2.0 A at 12 V for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the expected temperature rise if no heat is lost to the surroundings. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg°C.
practice_questions.marks: Energy supplied: \(E = VIt = 12 \times 2.0 \times 300 = 7200\) J (1). Rearrange \(\Delta E = mc\Delta T\): \(\Delta T = \Delta E \div (mc) = 7200 \div (0.80 \times 900) = 7200 \div 720 = 10\)°C (1). Correct substitution with units shown (1). Final answer 10°C (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the particle model, why the temperature of water stays at 100°C while it is boiling, even though a heater is still supplying energy.
practice_questions.marks: At boiling point the supplied energy goes into breaking the forces of attraction between water molecules (1), allowing molecules to escape from the liquid and become gas particles (1). None of the energy goes into increasing the kinetic energy of the particles, so the temperature does not rise (1).

practice_questions.text: Calculate the energy needed to convert 0.25 kg of water at 100°C completely into steam at 100°C. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2 260 000 J/kg.
practice_questions.marks: \(E = mL = 0.25 \times 2\,260\,000 = 565\,000\) J (1). Unit correct: J or kJ stated (1).

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the specific heat capacity of water. She heats 0.50 kg of water using a 50 W immersion heater for 4.0 minutes and records a temperature rise of 11°C. Calculate the specific heat capacity from her results and suggest one reason why it differs from the accepted value of 4200 J/kg°C.
practice_questions.marks: Energy supplied: \(E = P \times t = 50 \times 240 = 12\,000\) J (1). \(c = E \div (m \times \Delta T) = 12\,000 \div (0.50 \times 11) = 12\,000 \div 5.5 \approx 2180\) J/kg°C (1). Calculated value is lower than accepted value (1). Reason: heat is lost to the surroundings / the container / the air, so not all energy goes into the water (1). Evaluation of experimental design — e.g. adding insulation or a lid would reduce heat loss (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how the density of water changes as it cools from liquid to solid (ice), and explain this behaviour using the particle model.
practice_questions.marks: Water's density increases as it cools from room temperature toward 4°C (1), but then decreases as it solidifies — ice is less dense than liquid water (1). In ice, water molecules form a more open crystalline structure with more space between them than in liquid water, so the same mass occupies a larger volume and density is lower (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What happens to the temperature of a substance during a change of state?
options: It rises steadily as energy is added
It stays constant because energy is used to change particle arrangement
It falls because energy is being absorbed

knowledge_checks.q: A material has a specific heat capacity of 385 J/kg°C. How much energy is needed to raise 2 kg of this material by 10°C?
The energy required to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature is called _____ heat.
In the equation \(\Delta E = mc\Delta T\), the symbol \(c\) represents the _____ of the material.
Match each term to its definition.
right: Energy needed to boil a liquid at constant temperature per kilogram
Total kinetic and potential energy of all particles in a substance
A scientific model describing matter as tiny particles in constant motion
Energy to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C

flashcard_questions.q: What is the specific heat capacity of water?
Write the equation linking energy, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change.
Write the equation linking energy, mass and specific latent heat.
In which state are particles held in fixed positions and can only vibrate?
Why does temperature stay constant during melting?
flashcard_questions.a: Energy breaks bonds between particles rather than increasing their kinetic energy.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the internal energy of a substance?
flashcard_questions.a: The total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles.

flashcard_questions.q: Which is larger — the specific latent heat of fusion or vaporisation for the same substance?
flashcard_questions.a: Vaporisation, because all intermolecular forces must be fully overcome.

flashcard_questions.q: What fills in the blank: Cloze: Density = _____ ÷ volume.
Why does ice float on water?
flashcard_questions.a: Ice has a lower density than liquid water because its crystalline structure takes up more space.

flashcard_questions.q: What two types of energy make up the internal energy of a substance?
flashcard_questions.a: Kinetic energy (particle motion) and potential energy (forces between particles).

flashcard_questions.q: What does a high specific heat capacity tell you about a material?
flashcard_questions.a: It stores a large amount of energy per kilogram per degree of temperature rise.

flashcard_questions.q: In the PAG measurement of specific heat capacity, why should you insulate the sample?
flashcard_questions.a: To reduce heat loss to the surroundings and make the results more accurate.

glossary_terms.definition: A scientific model describing matter as composed of tiny particles in constant motion, with properties depending on how closely packed and freely they move.
A state of matter in which particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement and can only vibrate about fixed positions.
A state of matter in which particles are close together but can slide past each other, giving a definite volume but no fixed shape.
A state of matter in which particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions, filling any container they occupy.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a substance.
A change from one physical state to another — for example, melting or boiling — that occurs at a fixed temperature.
The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a material by 1°C, measured in J/kg°C.
The energy required to change the state of a substance at constant temperature, without raising its temperature.
The energy per kilogram needed to melt a solid or freeze a liquid at constant temperature.
The energy per kilogram needed to boil a liquid or condense a gas at constant temperature.
